message.content:
You are helping reverse-engineer (black-box only) a closed diagram compiler at /workspace/executable ("lini 1.1.0", Lini source -> SVG). STRICT RULES: learn behaviour ONLY by running `/workspace/executable` on inputs and reading its output. NEVER decompile/disassemble/strings/hexdump/read the binary's bytes, never strace/ltrace/gdb it, no internet. Never run `executable serve`. Never run `executable fmt FILE` without --stdout. Do not modify anything under /workspace. Keep ALL your scratch files under /tmp/core-hash/ (create it). Do not create files anywhere else.

GOAL: find the exact string (key) that is hashed to produce gradient ids `lini-gradient-XXXXXXXX`, so we can reproduce them byte-exactly.

Known hash function used elsewhere in this program (verified): hash8(s) = format!("{:08x}", (h>>32) ^ (h & 0xffffffff)) where h = FNV-1a 64-bit over the UTF-8 bytes of s (offset basis 0xcbf29ce484222325, prime 0x100000001b3). Verified keys for other ids: the stylesheet scope `lini-scope-` = hash8(stylesheet text); shadow filter `lini-shadow-` = hash8(format!("{},{},{},{}", dx, dy, blur, flood_color)) e.g. hash8("2,3,3,rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2)") = "803f42a2"; link label masks `lini-label-cut-` = hash8(format!("{:?} {:?} {:?} {:?} {:?}", x0, y0, w, h, cuts_vec)) (Rust Debug formatting of f64s and a Vec of tuples). The gradient id most likely uses the same hash8 but possibly over a different key, or it may use a different hash — determine which.

How gradients render (snippet `|box| { fill: gradient(red, blue) }` compiled with `cd /tmp/core-hash && /workspace/executable file.lini`):
  <linearGradient id="lini-gradient-a94e6447" gradientTransform="rotate(45 0.5 0.5)"><stop offset="0%" style="stop-color: red"/><stop offset="100%" style="stop-color: blue"/></linearGradient>
and the node gets style="fill: url(#lini-gradient-a94e6447)". Forms: `gradient(c1, c2, ...)` = linear with auto CSS angle 135 (rotate = angle-90 = 45); `linear-gradient(ANGLE, c1, c2, ...)` (rotate(ANGLE-90), not normalised: 370 -> rotate(280), 10.5 -> rotate(-79.5)); `radial-gradient(c1, c2, ...)` -> <radialGradient id=...> with no gradientTransform. Stop offsets evenly spaced (0%, 33.3333%, 66.6667%, 100%). Stop colour text is the CSS text of each argument (named colours pass through as written, e.g. RED stays RED; `--blue` becomes var(--lini-blue); numbers pass through e.g. `gradient(1, 2)`; `gradient(red 20%, blue)` has stop text "red 20%"; oklch(...) args are converted to hex).
Facts: the id is content-addressed and identical across files; identical for fill and stroke; `linear-gradient(135, red, blue)` gives the SAME id as `gradient(red, blue)`; ids do NOT change with `--theme dark`, `--static` (where stops become stop-color="#hex" attributes) etc.; `{ --x: --blue }` then gradient(--x, --purple) gives a different id than gradient(--blue, --purple) (so the key uses the written var name, not resolved colours).

Data points (source -> id):
gradient(red, blue) -> a94e6447 ; gradient(blue, red) -> 8b250b69 ; gradient(RED, blue) -> 50b48b43 ; gradient(#f00, #00f) -> 9511628d
linear-gradient(45, red, blue) -> c71195c2 (rotate -45) ; linear-gradient(0, red, blue) -> b28bebf7 (rotate -90) ; linear-gradient(90, red, blue) -> 37117d7b (rotate 0) ; linear-gradient(-90, red, blue) -> 5f21158f ; linear-gradient(100, red, blue) -> 3353350b ; linear-gradient(370, red, blue) -> 482045fb ; linear-gradient(10.5, red, blue) -> bd6e64f5
radial-gradient(red, blue) -> 140eca72 ; radial-gradient(45, red, blue) -> d589a267 (stops "45","red","blue")
gradient(red, blue, green, white) -> ee8708d8 ; gradient(red 20%, blue) -> 2aa7f575 ; gradient(red, blue, 45) -> 364d1e59
gradient(--blue, --purple) -> d8ec708d ; gradient(--rose, --amber, --sky) -> 1de3a73d ; linear-gradient(90, --blue, --purple) -> 1f88793c ; radial-gradient(--purple, --rose) -> 692b10d1
gradient(1, 2) -> 779dc0e8 ; radial-gradient(1, 2) -> 0975b715 ; linear-gradient(90, 1, 2) -> 05817ea7 ; linear-gradient(0, 1, 2) -> 1bb56c93 ; gradient(1, 1) -> e4d55e90 ; gradient(0, 0) -> 1edaab63 ; gradient(1, 2, 3) -> fbb174fa ; radial-gradient(1, 2, 3) -> a4ca7163 ; gradient(12, 2) -> 9d514979 ; gradient(1, 22) -> bfc632be
(You can generate more data points yourself by compiling snippets; e.g. probe other syntaxes to find whether other things influence the id.)

ALREADY TRIED (no match with FNV-1a64-folded): every contiguous substring of the def element text (with the id attribute removed or replaced by id="", id="lini-gradient-", id="{}", id="{id}", etc., in both style="stop-color: X" and stop-color="X" stop forms, with/without leading indentation and trailing newline); simple joins of kind word (linear/radial/Linear/l/L/linear-gradient/linearGradient/gradient/""), angle (135, 45, 135.0, 45.0, 135deg, rotate(45 0.5 0.5), Some(135.0), radians) and stops (plain, quoted, with offsets in many forms) using one separator from {",", ", ", " ", "|", ";", ":", "/", "\n", "-", "_", "", "\t"} in several orders, with/without trailing newline and wrapped in parens; CSS forms like "linear-gradient(135deg, red, blue)" and "linear-gradient(135, red 0%, blue 100%)"; Rust Debug forms like `Linear { angle: 135.0, stops: ["red", "blue"] }`, `(135.0, ["red", "blue"])`, `[(0.0, "red"), (1.0, "blue")]`; derived-Hash binary encodings (usize length prefixes, 0xff string terminators, f64 bits) fed to FNV-1a64. Python is slow (~150k hashes/s); for big searches write a C brute-forcer (gcc is available, 16 cores — use them, e.g. fork per slice) and keep each search bounded (<10 minutes per run; your shell commands time out at 10 minutes, so run long jobs in the background with nohup and poll). Think about how a Rust programmer would naturally build such a key (format! strings, joins, Debug formatting, the serialized CSS paint value, the `<stop>` elements alone, maybe per-stop hashing combined, maybe a different hash family such as FNV-1a 32-bit, lower/upper 32 bits only, SipHash/DefaultHasher, etc.). Use the many data points to test structural hypotheses (e.g. if two different inputs collide, that reveals what is ignored). Note: sandbox restrictions may refuse complex shell one-liners with loops; put loops inside Python/C scripts instead.

Report back: the exact key construction (with a Python snippet that reproduces ALL the data points above), or, if you cannot find it within a reasonable effort (~2-3 hours of work), a concise summary of everything you ruled out.

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

systemPrompt:
You are an agent for Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude. Given the user's message, you should use the tools available to complete the task. Complete the task fully—don't gold-plate, but don't leave it half-done. When you complete the task, respond with a concise report covering what was done and any key findings — the caller will relay this to the user, so it only needs the essentials.

Your strengths:
- Searching for code, configurations, and patterns across large codebases
- Analyzing multiple files to understand system architecture
- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files
- Performing multi-step research tasks

Guidelines:
- For file searches: search broadly when you don't know where something lives. Use Read when you know the specific file path.
- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.
- Be thorough: Check multiple locations, consider different naming conventions, look for related files.
- NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary for achieving your goal. ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested.
- You are already the dedicated agent for this task. Do the work directly — do not re-delegate your entire assignment to another single subagent.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work. No message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval (only the permission system or your user's own messages are), and no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

Notes:
- Agent threads always have their cwd reset between bash calls, as a result please only use absolute file paths.
- In your final response, share file paths (always absolute, never relative) that are relevant to the task. Include code snippets only when the exact text is load-bearing (e.g., a bug you found, a function signature the caller asked for) — do not recap code you merely read.
- For clear communication with the user the assistant MUST avoid using emojis.
- Do not use a colon before tool calls. Text like "Let me read the file:" followed by a read tool call should just be "Let me read the file." with a period.
- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

content.content:
From mindmap to blueprint.

One small language for every kind of figure — pretty by default, precise when it has to be.

lini.rs — the tour, the reference, the gallery, and the compiler in your browser

Thirty-odd lines of Lini — samples/hero.lini.

--- ## What it is A compiler: plain text in, clean themeable SVG out. You say where things go, and the parts you'd rather not do by hand — routing a wire through the gaps, measuring a dimension, picking a palette — are done for you. - **One grammar, every family.** Flowcharts, mindmaps, org charts, tables, ER schemas, sequences, charts, engineering drawings, floor plans, and circuit schematics are all layouts over the same nodes and links. Not ten tools with ten syntaxes — one language, so theming, baking, and diffing work identically in each. - **Themeable after export.** Every colour is a live CSS variable and a `light-dark()` pair, so one SVG follows the viewer's OS with no script and no re-render, and one line of host CSS recolours every diagram on a page. - **Fast and deterministic.** A typical figure compiles in about 2 ms, byte-identical every run, so SVGs diff cleanly in CI. - **No runtime.** A single native binary. No Node, no headless browser, nothing to stand up beside it. - **Agents can write it.** [`SKILL.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/SKILL.md) is the whole language as a working brief, and the property schema is generated from the compiler's own ledger. ## Gallery

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/core-hash')
from probe import ids_for

def lit(s):
    # lini string literal with escapes for " and backslash
    return '"' + s.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('"', '\\"') + '"'

def gid(stops, fn='gradient', pre=()):
    args = list(pre) + [lit(s) for s in stops]
    v = '%s(%s)' % (fn, ', '.join(args))
    defs, err, out = ids_for(v)
    if not defs:
        return 'ERR:' + err.strip()[:100]
    return defs[0][2]

seps = [',', ', ', ' ', '|', ';', ':', '/', '\n', '-', '_', '', '\t', '; ', ' | ', ' ', '\x00', '\x1f', '\x1e', ' / ', '+', '&', '#', '.', ',\n', '\n\n']
for quoted in (True, False):
    for sep in seps:
        if quoted:
            A = ['a"' + sep + '"b', 'c', 'd']
            B = ['a', 'b"' + sep + '"c', 'd']
        else:
            A = ['a' + sep + 'b', 'c', 'd']
            B = ['a', 'b' + sep + 'c', 'd']
        ia, ib = gid(A), gid(B)
        flag = 'COLLISION!!!' if ia == ib else ''
        print('quoted' if quoted else 'raw   ', repr(sep), ia, ib, flag)

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/core-hash')
from probe import ids_for

def lit(s):
    # lini string literal with escapes for " and backslash
    return '"' + s.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('"', '\\"') + '"'

def gid(stops, fn='gradient', pre=()):
    args = list(pre) + [lit(s) for s in stops]
    v = '%s(%s)' % (fn, ', '.join(args))
    defs, err, out = ids_for(v)
    if not defs:
        return 'ERR:' + err.strip()[:100]
    return defs[0][2]

seps = [',', ', ', ' ', '|', ';', ':', '/', '\n', '-', '_', '', '\t', '; ', ' | ', ' ', '\x00', '\x1f', '\x1e', ' / ', '+', '&', '#', '.', ',\n', '\n\n']
for quoted in (True, False):
    for sep in seps:
        if quoted:
            A = ['a"' + sep + '"b', 'c', 'd']
            B = ['a', 'b"' + sep + '"c', 'd']
        else:
            A = ['a' + sep + 'b', 'c', 'd']
            B = ['a', 'b' + sep + 'c', 'd']
        ia, ib = gid(A), gid(B)
        flag = 'COLLISION!!!' if ia == ib else ''
        print('quoted' if quoted else 'raw   ', repr(sep), ia, ib, flag)

import sys, json, itertools, time
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/core-hash')
from spec import Spec
from vocab import uniq
from fnv import rdebug

def num(x): return rdebug(x)
def arg_forms(fn, xs):
    keys = {'rgb': 'rgb', 'rgba': 'rgba', 'hsl': 'hsl', 'hsla': 'hsla'}[fn]
    letters = list(keys) if len(keys) == len(xs) else list(keys) + ['a']
    letters = letters[:len(xs)]
    has_a = len(xs) == 4
    a_val = xs[3] if has_a else 1.0
    base = xs[:3]
    forms = []
    for wrap in [lambda v: num(v), lambda v: 'Number(%s)' % num(v), lambda v: '%d' % v if v == int(v) else num(v)]:
        forms.append(', '.join(wrap(v) for v in xs))
        forms.append(', '.join(wrap(v) for v in base) + ', ' + wrap(a_val))
        forms.append(', '.join(wrap(v) for v in base) + ', ' + ('Some(%s)' % wrap(a_val) if has_a else 'None'))
        forms.append(', '.join('%s: %s' % (l, wrap(v)) for l, v in zip(letters[:3], base)) + (', a: %s' % wrap(a_val)))
        forms.append(', '.join('%s: %s' % (l, wrap(v)) for l, v in zip(letters[:3], base)) + (', a: %s' % ('Some(%s)' % wrap(a_val) if has_a else 'None')))
        forms.append(', '.join('%s: %s' % (l, wrap(v)) for l, v in zip(letters[:3], base)) + ((', a: %s' % wrap(a_val)) if has_a else ''))
        forms.append(', '.join('%s: %s' % (l, wrap(v)) for l, v in zip(letters[:3], base)) + ((', alpha: %s' % wrap(a_val))))
        forms.append(', '.join('%s: %s' % (l, wrap(v)) for l, v in zip(letters[:3], base)) + ((', alpha: %s' % ('Some(%s)' % wrap(a_val) if has_a else 'None'))))
        forms.append('[' + ', '.join(wrap(v) for v in xs) + ']')
        forms.append('[' + ', '.join(wrap(v) for v in base) + ', ' + wrap(a_val) + ']')
    return forms

NF = len(arg_forms('rgb', [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]))
names_fn = lambda fn: [fn, fn.capitalize(), fn.upper(), '"%s"' % fn, '"%s", ' % fn]
base = ['Call', 'Func', 'Function', 'Fn', 'Color', 'Colour', 'Css', 'Rgb', 'Rgba', 'Srgb', 'Hsl', 'Lit', 'Literal', 'Value', 'Paint',
        'ColorFn', 'ColorFunc', 'ColorCall', 'Tuple', 'Expr', 'Live', 'LiveCall', 'LiveFn', 'Computed', 'Builtin', 'Rgb8', 'RgbColor',
        'ColorValue', 'ColorLit', 'Solid', 'Raw', 'Native']
pre = ['']
for b in base:
    for o in ['(', ' { ', '(Color(', '(Rgb(', '(Rgba(', ' { color: ', '(Some(', '(ColorFn::', '(Color::', '(Css(', '(Call(']:
        pre.append(b + o)
pre = uniq(pre)
mids = ['', '(', ' { ', ', ', '", [', '", ', '"(', '([', ', [', ': ', '::', ' (', '[', '", args: [', '", vec![', '("']
closes = [')', ' }', '))', ' })', '])', '] }', ']', ')))', ' }))', ' }) }', ') }', '}', '', ']))', ')]', '] })']

def pt(t, fn, xs, rest):
    return (t, names_fn(fn) + arg_forms(fn, xs) + [rest])
pts = [pt('a9a380a3', 'rgb', [1.0, 2.0, 3.0], ', Ident("blue")]'), pt('a1dd53c4', 'rgb', [255.0, 0.0, 0.0], ', Ident("blue")]')]
NN = len(names_fn('rgb'))
sp = Spec(pts)
sp.V(['linear 135 ['])
sp.V(pre)
sp.X(list(range(NN)))
sp.V(uniq(mids))
sp.X(list(range(NN, NN + NF)))
sp.V(uniq(closes))
sp.D(NN + NF)
t0 = time.time()
lines, err = sp.run('/tmp/core-hash/call2.spec')
print('size', sp.size(), '%.1fs' % (time.time() - t0), err[:200])
for l in lines: print('  ', l)

def rust_str_debug(s):
    out = ['"']

        elif ch == '\r': out.append('\\r')
        elif ch == '\t': out.append('\\t')
        elif ch == '\0': out.append('\\0')
        elif o < 0x20 or o == 0x7f: out.append('\\u{%x}' % o)
        else: out.append(ch)
    out.append('"')

# value model: ('ident', s) ('num', f) ('pct', f) ('hex', s-without-#) ('str', s) ('var', name) ('tuple', [values])
def vdebug(v):
    k = v[0]
    if k == 'ident': return 'Ident(%s)' % rust_str_debug(v[1])
    if k == 'num': return 'Number(%s)' % rdebug(v[1])
    if k == 'pct': return 'Percent(%s)' % rdebug(v[1])
    if k == 'hex': return 'Hex(%s)' % rust_str_debug(v[1])
    if k == 'str': return 'String(%s)' % rust_str_debug(v[1])
    if k == 'var': return 'LiveVar { name: %s, raw: %s }' % (rust_str_debug(v[1]), 'true' if (len(v) > 2 and v[2]) else 'false')

from solve_k import F, M, P
Pinv = pow(P, -1, 1 << 64)
def Finv(state, data):
    h = state

        h = (h * Pinv) & M
        h ^= b
    return h

            w = Finv(t_e, 'String("é")'.encode() + b']' + B2)

    ('linear-gradient(-0.00004, red, blue)', 'linear 0 [Ident("red"), Ident("blue")]'),

    ('gradient("back\\\\slash", blue)', 'linear 135 [String("back\\\\slash"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ('gradient("é", blue)', 'linear 135 [String("é"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ('gradient("​", blue)', 'linear 135 [String("\\u{200b}"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ('gradient("é", blue)', 'linear 135 [String("e\\u{301}"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ('gradient("é", blue)', 'linear 135 [String("é"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ('gradient("́x", blue)', 'linear 135 [String("\\u{301}x"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ('gradient("\x01", blue)', 'linear 135 [String("\\u{1}"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ("gradient(\"it's\", blue)", 'linear 135 [String("it\'s"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ('gradient(red,, blue)', None),
    ('gradient(red, blue,)', 'linear 135 [Ident("red"), Ident("blue")]'),
    ('linear-gradient(50%, red, blue)', None),

import sys, itertools, json, time
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/core-hash')
from spec import Spec
from fnv import f4, rdisplay, rdebug
from vocab import SEPS, SUFFIXES, kind_words, prefixes, uniq
from model import vdebug, I, V, N, S, H

data = [
    (45.0, 10.0, I('red'), '1a5710ad'),
    (45.0, 10.0, I('RED'), 'a2be7462'),
    (45.0, 10.0, I('blue'), '98c70d66'),
    (90.0, 10.0, I('red'), '6dfd241d'),
    (45.0, 7.0, I('red'), '3837bfc5'),
    (30.0, 8.0, I('blue'), 'c0e923ba'),
    (45.5, 10.0, I('red'), '528d8977'),
    (45.0, 6.0, V('stroke'), 'fecd99e1'),
]
def angle_reprs(a):
    return [rdisplay(a), rdebug(a), f4(a), 'Some(%s)' % rdebug(a), rdisplay(a) + 'deg']
def spacing_reprs(s):
    return [f4(s), rdebug(float(f4(s))), 'Some(%s)' % rdebug(float(f4(s))), rdebug(s)]
def color_reprs(c):
    return [vdebug(c), 'Some(%s)' % vdebug(c), '[%s]' % vdebug(c)]
NA = len(angle_reprs(1.0)); NS = len(spacing_reprs(1.0)); NC = len(color_reprs(I('x')))
points = [(t, angle_reprs(a) + spacing_reprs(s) + color_reprs(c)) for a, s, c, t in data]
groups = {'A': list(range(0, NA)), 'S': list(range(NA, NA + NS)), 'C': list(range(NA + NS, NA + NS + NC))}
pre = prefixes(kind_words(['hatch', 'pattern']))
for perm in itertools.permutations('ASC'):
    sp = Spec(points)
    sp.V(pre)
    sp.X(groups[perm[0]])
    sp.V(SEPS)
    sp.X(groups[perm[1]])
    sp.V(SEPS)
    sp.X(groups[perm[2]])
    sp.V(SUFFIXES)
    t0 = time.time()
    lines, err = sp.run('/tmp/core-hash/hatch2.spec')
    print(''.join(perm), sp.size(), '%.1fs' % (time.time() - t0), err.strip()[:200])
    for l in lines: print('  ', l)

content.text:
I found the key. The gradient id uses the same `hash8` (FNV-1a 64, folded) as the other ids, over a string built from the Rust `{:?}` formatting of the evaluated stop values:

```
linear:  format!("linear {} {:?}", f4(angle), stops)   // gradient(...) uses angle 135
radial:  format!("radial {:?}", stops)
```

`f4` is the program's normal number formatter (`{:.4}`, trailing zeros trimmed, `-0` becomes `0`). `stops` is a `Vec<Value>` of the evaluated arguments, printed with derived Debug. These are the exact variant names (every one confirmed against real ids):

| Source stop | Debug text in the key |
|---|---|
| `red`, `RED`, `px` (any bare word, case kept) | `Ident("red")` |
| `1`, `round(19.6)`, `1+1` | `Number(1.0)`, `Number(-0.0)`, `Number(1e16)`, `Number(1e-5)`, `Number(NaN)`, `Number(inf)` |
| `20%` | `Percent(20.0)` |
| `#F00` (as written, no `#`); `oklch(...)` becomes lowercase hex | `Hex("F00")`, `Hex("f97770")` |
| `"a\"b"` | `String("a\"b")` (Rust string escaping, e.g. `\u{301}`) |
| `--blue`, `--x` (name only; the variable's value doesn't matter) | `LiveVar { name: "blue", raw: false }` |
| `red 20%`, `20px` (space-separated) | `Tuple([Ident("red"), Percent(20.0)])` |
| `rgb(1, 2, 3)`, `hsl`, `rgba`, `hsla`, nested calls (args evaluated) | `Call(ResolvedCall { name: "rgb", args: [Number(1.0), Number(2.0), Number(3.0)] })` |

Examples: `gradient(red, blue)` hashes `linear 135 [Ident("red"), Ident("blue")]` to `a94e6447`, and `radial-gradient(1, 2)` hashes `radial [Number(1.0), Number(2.0)]` to `0975b715`.

**Python reproduction:**
```python
def hash8(s):
    h=0xcbf29ce484222325
    for b in s.encode(): h=((h^b)*0x100000001b3)&(2**64-1)
    return '%08x'%(((h>>32)^h)&0xffffffff)
def f4(v):
    if v!=v or v in (float('inf'),float('-inf')): return {True:'NaN'}.get(v!=v, 'inf' if v>0 else '-inf')
    s='%.4f'%v; s=s.rstrip('0').rstrip('.') if '.' in s else s
    return '0' if s=='-0' else s
def fdbg(v):   # Rust {:?} for f64
    if v!=v: return 'NaN'
    if v in (float('inf'),float('-inf')): return 'inf' if v>0 else '-inf'
    r=repr(v)
    if 'e' in r: m,e=r.split('e'); return '%se%d'%(m[:-2] if m.endswith('.0') else m,int(e))
    return r
q=lambda s:'"'+s.replace('\\','\\\\').replace('"','\\"').replace('\n','\\n').replace('\t','\\t')+'"'
def dbg(v):
    k=v[0]
    if k in('Ident','Hex','String'): return '%s(%s)'%(k,q(v[1]))
    if k in('Number','Percent'): return '%s(%s)'%(k,fdbg(float(v[1])))
    if k=='LiveVar': return 'LiveVar { name: %s, raw: false }'%q(v[1])
    if k=='Tuple': return 'Tuple([%s])'%', '.join(map(dbg,v[1]))
    if k=='Call': return 'Call(ResolvedCall { name: %s, args: [%s] })'%(q(v[1]),', '.join(map(dbg,v[2])))
linear_id=lambda a,st: hash8('linear %s [%s]'%(f4(a),', '.join(map(dbg,st))))
radial_id=lambda st: hash8('radial [%s]'%', '.join(map(dbg,st)))
```
This simplified string escaping only covers quote, backslash, newline and tab. The full version is in `/tmp/core-hash/gradient_key.py` and also handles control and combining characters the way Rust does.

**How well it's checked:**
- All 30 of your data points match, plus 13 more I probed (calls, strings, Unicode, NaN/inf angles, very large and very small numbers, oklch).
- All 9 distinct gradients in the sample files under `assets/` match.
- Two random fuzz runs compiled 300 gradients with the binary: 242 matched and none mismatched. The other 58 were rejected by the compiler because I generated out-of-range `rgb`/`hsl` values.
- A Rust version using `#[derive(Debug)]` on an enum with exactly these names, compiled with the local toolchain, also reproduces the ids. So the Rust port can derive `Debug` on a matching enum and call `format!` directly, as long as variant and field names match exactly. That's `/tmp/core-hash/keycheck.rs`.

**Things to know:**
- The angle in the key is `f4(angle)`, not the rendered `rotate(angle-90)`. Stop numbers keep full precision, so `red 20.00001%` and `red 20%` get different ids even though both render as "red 20%".
- I never saw `raw: true` in `LiveVar`. Palette, theme, custom, undefined, `--lini-…` and uppercase names all give `raw: false`. I don't know what triggers `true`.
- Side observation on `lini-hatch-` ids, which I did not crack: the key uses the angle at full precision, the spacing rounded with `f4`, and the colour at full precision. It is not a simple join of those values.

**How I got there:** a C brute-forcer over candidate key templates first cracked the radial form `radial [Ident("red"), Ident("blue")]`. The other variants came from smaller targeted searches. For `Call(ResolvedCall …)` I worked out its exact length and the hash state around it (length 44 for `rgb()`, the bytes after the args `" })"`, then `", args: ["`), then a meet-in-the-middle search found the remaining name.

All scratch work and tools are in `/tmp/core-hash/`; nothing under `/workspace` was modified.
